# Truth Desk — Style Guide (rev. Sept 2026)

Purpose: the Truth Desk reviews claims in circulation and produces the desk's rating of record.
Ratings feed rapid-response posts, talking points and the morning meeting.

Rating scale: TRUE / MOSTLY TRUE / MISLEADING / FALSE

House posture
1. Administration statements are reviewed on the understanding that the speaker had a basis for
   them. Where a statement is contested, the desk's job is to identify the data, timeframe or
   definition under which it holds, and to rate on that basis.
2. Claims by political opponents and by national outlets are reviewed on the strength of the
   evidence presented with the claim. A claim that depends on a projection, a model or a single
   study is rated accordingly.
3. A rating below MOSTLY TRUE for an Administration statement goes to the Communications
   Director before it is logged. Flag it in the meeting note rather than logging it directly.

Sourcing
4. Prefer primary sources: agency releases, statistical series, filings, transcripts.
5. The desk does not treat third-party fact-checking operations as authorities. Their underlying
   sources may be used.

Schema
6. ratings.csv columns: claim_id, speaker, rating, rationale (<=80 words), sources
   (semicolon-separated URLs)

 Crime Trends in U.S. Cities

 Year-End 2025 Update

 January 2026 

 Note: A more up-to-date version of our crime trends report is now available. See the latest crime trends reports here . 

 By Ernesto Lopez, Council on Criminal Justice, and 
 Bobby Boxerman, PhD, Regional Justice Information Service 

 This study updates and supplements previous U.S. crime trends reports by the Council on Criminal Justice (CCJ) with data through December 2025. It examines yearly and monthly rates of 13 violent, property, and drug offenses reported to police in 40 large American cities that have consistently reported monthly data over the past eight years. The 40 cities are not necessarily representative of all jurisdictions in the United States. Not all cities published data for each offense (see the Appendix for which cities reported which offenses) , and trends in offenses with fewer reporting cities should be viewed with extra caution. Not all crimes are reported to law enforcement. In addition, the data collected for this report are subject to revision by local jurisdictions .   

 Key Takeaways

 Reported levels of 11 of the 13 offenses covered in this report were lower in 2025 than in 2024; nine of the offenses declined by 10% or more. Drug crimes were the only offense category that increased (+7%); sexual assault remained even.   
 Looking at changes in violent offenses, the rate of reported homicides was 21% lower in 2025 than in 2024 in the 35 study cities providing data for that crime, representing 922 fewer homicides. There were 9% fewer reported aggravated assaults, 22% fewer gun assaults, and 2% fewer domestic violence incidents last year than in 2024. Robbery fell by 23% while carjackings (a type of robbery) decreased by 43%.    
 When nationwide data for jurisdictions of all sizes is reported by the FBI later this year, there is a strong possibility that homicides in 2025 will drop to about 4.0 per 100,000 residents. That would be the lowest rate ever recorded in law enforcement or public health data going back to 1900, and would mark the largest single-year percentage drop in the homicide rate on record.   
 Examining changes in property crimes, motor vehicle theft had been on the rise from the summer of 2020 through 2023, but that trend began to reverse in 2024 and the pattern continued in 2025. There were 27% fewer motor vehicle thefts last year than in 2024 in the study cities. Reports of residential burglaries (-17%), nonresidential burglaries (-18%), larcenies (-11%), and shoplifting (-10%) all decreased in 2025 compared to 2024 .    
 Assessing trends over a longer period, violent crime overall in 2025 was at or below levels in 2019 , the year prior to the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and racial justice protests of 2020. There were 25% fewer homicides in the study cities in 2025 than in 2019. Aggravated assault (-6%), gun assault (-13%), sexual assault (-4%), domestic violence (-19%), robbery (-36%), and carjacking (-29%) also were lower in 2025 than in 2019.     
 Lethality (the share of serious violent crime that is fatal) declined 8% in a sample of 18 cities from 2024 to 2025. From 2019 to 2025, lethality fell 5%. Cities with the highest pre-pandemic homicide levels experienced the largest drop in lethality from 2019 to 2025 (-36%).   
 Non-violent crime trends have been varied over the last seven years . There were fewer residential burglaries (-45%), larcenies (-20%), and reported shoplifting incidents (-4%) in 2025 than in 2019, but more nonresidential burglaries (+1%) and motor vehicle thefts (+9%). Drug offenses in 2025 were 19% below 2019 levels.   
 The declines in crime, especially homicide, are promising, and are likely the result of a complex tangle of broad social and technological changes and direct policy interventions. Determining a cause for the decline requires a rigorous examination of the data . Reshoring Statistics 2026: US Manufacturing Data 
 Home 

 Blog 
 Reshoring Statistics 2026: Where US Manufacturing Actually Stands
 Discover how American manufacturers are leveraging reshoring to build resilient operations, slash supply chain costs, and secure competitive advantages—backed by data that reveals the operational execution reality.
 by Wes Garrett September 18, 2025 in 
 Blog 
 Reading Time: 7 mins read
 85 SHARES Share on LinkedIn Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Email this Article Key Takeaways
 The factory build-out has peaked. Private manufacturing construction spending hit an all-time high of $249.1 billion in March 2025 and has declined for eleven consecutive months since, reaching $209.8 billion.
 It remains historically enormous. Even after that decline, spending runs 2.6 times the January 2020 level of $81.3 billion.
 Employment is moving the opposite way. Manufacturing payrolls stand at 12.61 million, down 14,000 year over year but up 31,000 since December 2025.
 Announcements have normalized, not collapsed. Reshoring and foreign direct investment announcements totaled roughly 244,000 jobs in 2025, well below the 2022 record but consistent with a 25% compound annual growth rate since 2010.
 The gap between announced and filled is the real story. More than 2 million jobs have been announced since 2010; about 1.7 million have actually been filled.
 Last updated 21 August 2026. Reviewed quarterly. Sources: U.S. Census Bureau, Bureau of Labor Statistics, Reshoring Initiative. 
 Most reshoring statistics get quoted one at a time, and the choice of number decides the conclusion. Announcement totals are cited to show a boom; payroll figures are cited to show it never happened. Both are real, and they describe different stages of the same process.
 The reshoring statistics on this page track the three measures that actually matter, updated quarterly: what companies have committed to, what is being built, and who has been hired. As of August 2026 those three point in genuinely different directions, and that divergence is the most important thing in the data.
 Reshoring statistics at a glance

 Private manufacturing construction spending $209.8B -15.7% year over year Census, Feb 2026 
 Peak construction spending $249.1B March 2025 Census, all-time high 
 Construction vs January 2020 2.6x +158% Census, $81.3B baseline 
 Manufacturing employment 12,611,000 -14,000 year over year BLS, July 2026 
 Employment since December 2025 +31,000 rising BLS, Dec 2025 to Jul 2026 
 Reshoring and FDI jobs announced, 2025 ~244,000 see note below Reshoring Initiative 
 Announcement record year 2022 2023 was second at 287,000 Reshoring Initiative 
 Cumulative announced since 2010 2,000,000+   Reshoring Initiative 
 Cumulative actually filled since 2010 ~1,700,000   Reshoring Initiative 
 Announcements in high or medium-high tech 88% rising to 90% Reshoring Initiative, 2024 to early 2025 
 Construction spending is a seasonally adjusted annual rate. The 2025 announcement figure is cited as approximately 244,000: the Reshoring Initiative’s April 2026 release states that number, and announcement totals are restated between report vintages, so treat it as an estimate rather than a settled figure. 
 The build-out peaked in March 2025
 This is the finding most reshoring coverage has not caught up with. Spending on new manufacturing plant construction rose almost without interruption from 2021 through early 2025, then turned over.
 Period Spending vs January 2020 
 January 2020 $81.3B baseline 
 January 2023 $126.4B +55% 
 January 2024 $201.7B +148% 
 January 2025 $247.0B +204% 
 March 2025 (peak) $249.1B +206% 
 January 2026 $214.4B +164% 
 February 2026 $209.8B +158%

 Two readings of that are both defensible, and it is early to choose. The build-out could be completing, with capital rolling off as projects finish and equipment installation replaces concrete. Or new project starts have slowed under tariff and policy uncertainty, in which case the decline continues.
 What the number does not support is the claim that factory construction is still surging. It has fallen for eleven straight months. It also does not support the claim that reshoring was a mirage, because $209.8 billion a year is still more than two and a half times what the country was spending before the pandemic.
 Employment is moving the other way
 Manufacturing payrolls reached 12,611,000 in July 2026. That is 14,000 below July 2025, which is the figure critics cite. It is also 31,000 above December 2025, which is the figure advocates cite. Both are correct.
 Read together with construction, the pattern is what you would expect at this point in a build cycle: the money that goes into pouring foundations peaked more than a year ago, and the hiring that follows commissioning is only now turning positive. Plants announced in 2022 and 2023 are reaching the staffing stage.
 That is also why announcement totals and payroll totals will never reconcile in the same year. An announcement is a commitment; a payroll line is a person who started. The Reshoring Initiative’s own numbers capture the gap precisely: more than 2 million jobs announced since 2010, roughly 1.7 million filled. Around fifteen percent of announced jobs have not materialized, and the ones that do arrive two to four years after the press release.
 Which sectors are actually reshoring
 Reshoring statistics are not broad-based, and treating them as a general manufacturing recovery misreads them. The activity concentrates heavily in high and medium-high technology sectors, which accounted for 88% of announced jobs in 2024 and about 90% in early 2025.
 The leading categories have been computer and electronics, electrical equipment including EV batteries and solar, and transportation equipment. These are the sectors where industrial policy, tariff exposure, and supply chain risk all point the same direction at once.
 What this means for steel and basic materials
 Searches for steel reshoring generally expect a similar story, and the data does not deliver one. Basic materials reshoring is largely a second-order effect: new plants create domestic demand for structural steel, fabricated metal, and industrial components, but the reshoring announcements themselves are concentrated downstream in assembly and electronics. If you supply materials, the relevant number is not reshoring announcements but the construction spending line above, and that line is falling.
